sentences.text: So today, we're moving on from generative models, and we're going to start talking about out-of-distribution generalization.
And this is, I think, one of the biggest open challenges for modern machine learning models, the ability to generalize to data that is not explicitly covered within the training distribution.
And so, just a bit of motivation here.
We've seen a lot of success in machine learning, right?
We have incredible models for image classification.
This is a aggregate of the ImageNet data set.
I would argue that, in many ways, things like simple categorization, the types of categorization we often try to do on data sets like ImageNet is pretty much solved.

There are, of course, a few corner cases that are pretty difficult, or sometimes, even erroneously labeled or ambiguous that are still hard for modern models within ImageNet, but mostly, it's a solved problem.
We've seen pretty great success on image generation.
We've been talking about that the last couple of days.
Strategy games, things like machine translation, robotic manipulation, we're starting to see success in all of these.
But then there are a lot of cases where machine learning still isn't very successful.
And sometimes, it can be surprising.
So I think one interesting example here is in the space of self-driving cars.
So we are starting to see self-driving cars be deployed.
I think Waymo in particular is starting to actually have fleets deployed in many different areas.
And of course, there's complicated dynamics around why we're not seeing self-driving cars at scale.
Regulation plays a huge role in that.
But I think one of the main reasons is because we really don't have a good mechanism to guarantee the robustness of these models.
We can't guarantee that they are not going to make potentially harmful mistakes.
And this really begs the question of, are these machine learning systems really ready for the real world?
And what dimensions of deployment in the real world are we still missing?
What do we need to be focusing on to be able to actually do this effectively?
And I do think there's an interesting point here, which is you could argue that a lot of machine learning is actually actively being deployed in the real world.
I think the GPT models is a great example of that.

People are using AI more and more day to day, but if I'm trying to characterize the types of AI that are ready for deployment versus the types of AI that, even if we try to deploy them, we invest billions of dollars into figuring out how to make them deployable, we're still not seeing
that progress or actually really seeing it happen, I think it comes down to risk.
A lot of the cases where we see AI models deployed are what I would characterize as high precision human verification systems.
So you need the model to be good enough to be useful, so it should work most of the time, but you also have a human verifier in the loop that is making corrections when something's not right.
So you have this verification loop that's always happening with human intelligence.
ChatGPT is a great example of this.
You prompt it with something.
You get a result. Maybe it's useful.
You probably edit it.
You probably interact with it in some way.
If it's just absolute trash, maybe you giggle about it, you share it with your friends, and then you prompt it with something completely different.
So there's this human brain that's in the loop, verifying that these things work well.
And things like hallucination aren't so much of an issue if a human is making the corrections themselves.
It's when we start trusting these models without being human verified that we start running into issues.
And I think another interesting example of that is things like a lot of the modern machine learning systems that are actively deployed in health care are what we call decision support tools.
So they're a tool that maybe a radiologist uses to try to highlight or potentially give some advice on what, maybe, a diagnosis could be.
And then the human is actually liable to verify that and make a decision.
And interestingly, there's been a bunch of fascinating work that's come out recently that really argues both sides of whether or not this is working.

There's research that showed that these decision support tools are really great for trying to make sure that patient outcomes are beneficial, that doctors aren't missing things, and then there's conflicting research that explicitly says that the deployment of these decision support tools is actively harming patient outcomes.
Because doctors are becoming compliant, they're not paying attention, and they're missing things in that long tail of the distribution that are actually quite important.
So the jury's still out.
And fascinatingly, if you look at the regulation around what it actually takes to deploy decision support tool in a hospital, the metrics are kind of shocking.
I'm not going to quote myself on the details, but essentially, it's like, you have to prove some percent accuracy on some small population of data.
But it's not nearly what you would expect.
I remember being quite surprised.
Something like on the order of like 100 or 1,000 patients to be able to deploy a decision support tool.

You're just trying to support the decision of an expert.
So, really, when we have this case, this is where we start to see things working well.

objectives.text: You'll be able to analyze how distribution shifts and adversarial examples expose the brittleness and weaknesses of deployed machine learning models.
You'll be able to explain how data biases and realistic distribution shifts impact generalization, and describe how Distributionally Robust Optimization (DRO) addresses these issues.

segments.subgoal: Analyze the real-world challenges of deploying robust machine learning models

key_points.text: Generalizing to data outside the training distribution (OOD) is one of the biggest open challenges in modern machine learning.
Many currently deployed AI systems, such as ChatGPT, rely on human verification loops to manage risks like hallucination.
A major barrier to scaling self-driving cars is the inability to guarantee the robustness of their machine learning models.
The deployment of decision support tools in healthcare is subject to conflicting research, with some studies showing harm to patient outcomes.

key_terms.definition: Out-of-distribution generalization is the ability of a machine learning model to generalize to data that was not explicitly covered within the training distribution. This ability is considered one of the biggest open challenges in modern machine learning.

Human verifier in the loop describes a deployment strategy where a human is actively involved in making corrections when an AI model's output is not right. This verification loop ensures that human intelligence is always present.

Decision support tools are machine learning systems that provide advice or highlight information, such as potential diagnoses. The human user is ultimately liable to verify the tool's output and make the final decision.

segments.subgoal: Analyze how distribution shifts cause model failure in real-world deployment

key_points.text: Standard machine learning assumes that training data is Independently and Identically Distributed (IID) to the data used for inference, but this is rarely true in the real world.
Distribution shifts can occur through various mechanisms, including data perturbation, changes in sensor systems, or shifts in the set of categories of interest.
The inability to anticipate every possible change in the world makes it impossible to collect sufficient, representative data for deployment.
Using off-the-shelf tools often assumes random splitting is sufficient, which can lead to falsely high performance expectations due to strong correlations in the data.

key_terms.definition: Independently and Identically Distributed (IID) is a theoretical assumption in machine learning where the data used for training a model is drawn from the same distribution as the data used for inference. This ideal setting requires that the training distribution equals the test distribution, a condition the instructor notes is rarely true in the real world.

Distributional change is a fundamental difference that occurs between the distribution of data used for training a model and the distribution of data encountered during deployment. This shift means the real-world data differs from the data the model was originally trained on.

Data poisoning is a failure mode where the evaluation of machine learning systems is constructed in a way that is artificially Independently and Identically Distributed (IID). This artificial construction fails to represent the true complexity or reality of the deployment environment.

segments.subgoal: Illustrate how adversarial examples demonstrate the brittleness of ML models

key_points.text: Adversarial examples involve adding small, optimized noise to an input to maximally change the model's prediction.
These examples highlight the brittleness of machine learning models, which are sensitive to changes invisible to humans.
Adversarial attacks can be applied to physical objects, 3D models, and speech waveforms.
Early research into adversarial examples began in 2004, with motivating examples including spam filters.

key_terms.definition: Adversarial example is a data point to which a small, optimized amount of noise is added, causing a machine learning model to change its prediction dramatically. This noise is explicitly designed to be maximally adversarial, even if the resulting image looks identical to a human observer.

segments.subgoal: Describe the process of generating adversarial examples using gradient ascent

key_points.text: Adversarial examples are small perturbations to an image that change the model's prediction without changing the meaning to a human.
The infinity norm is commonly used to constrain the perturbation, ensuring the largest change for any single pixel remains small.
Adversarial examples can be found using Projected Gradient Ascent, which updates the data perturbation over time.
Projected Gradient Ascent involves taking a step in the direction of the gradient and then projecting the result back into the feasible set.

key_terms.definition: Adversarial example is a small perturbation added to a given image that does not change the image's meaning to a human but successfully changes the classification meaning to a machine learning model. The goal is to find this perturbation to make the model predict a wrong, target category.

Perturbation is a small change applied to a given input image, which is designed to change the model's prediction without being noticeable to a human observer. This change is the variable that is optimized to maximize the model's misclassification.

Infinity norm is a constraint applied to the perturbation, ensuring that the largest change for any single pixel remains below a certain specified amount. This constraint helps result in changes that are unperceptible to humans.

Projected gradient ascent is a technique used to update the data perturbation over time by taking a step in the direction of the gradient and then projecting the result back into a feasible set. This process ensures the perturbation obeys the optimization constraint that the change cannot be too big

segments.subgoal: Compare methods for finding adversarial examples and introduce adversarial training

key_points.text: Some methods for finding adversarial examples, like projected gradient ascent, require access to the model weights and architecture to calculate gradients.
An alternative way to find an adversarial example is to maximize the loss between the model's prediction and the correct label, $y$, rather than maximizing the probability of a specific label.
Standard training minimizes loss over the model parameters ($\theta$), whereas adversarial training aims to make the model robust to expected perturbations.
Adversarial training involves nested optimization (two-loop) to find a model that remains effective even under the worst-case perturbation for every data point.

key_terms.definition: Adversarial example is an input modified by noise designed to maximize the loss between the model's prediction and the correct label. This approach focuses on finding the perturbation that makes the model most wrong, rather than forcing the model to predict a specific incorrect category.

Training adversarially is a method where the model is trained to be robust against expected perturbations by incorporating adversarial examples into the training process. This approach aims to make the model resilient to the types of noise it might encounter.

Nested optimization is a training framework involving two loops: an inner loop that finds the worst-case perturbation for a given image, and an outer loop that adjusts the model parameters to minimize the loss under that worst-case scenario.

segments.subgoal: Analyze how adversarial examples reveal model weaknesses and biases

key_points.text: Real-world data perturbations are often complex and not limited to the small amounts of static noise used in mathematical adversarial definitions.
Adversarial training involves a continuous loop where the model is trained against an approximate optimal adversarial perturbation of the data.
Adversarial examples demonstrate that models capture both robust features (semantically meaningful) and non-robust features (correlated with labels but easily flipped).
Correlative predictive features can exacerbate societal biases present in the training data, which is an ethical concern in machine learning.

key_terms.definition: Spurious correlation refers to features in the training data that are correlated with the label but are not semantically meaningful. These correlations allow a model to learn irrelevant signals, such as a specific pixel location, and ignore the rest of the input.

Adversarial robustness is the property of a model that allows it to remain stable when faced with adversarial perturbations. This concept relates to the model's ability to maintain correct predictions even when the input data is slightly altered.

Adversarial training is a process where, during the training loop, the model is trained against an approximate optimal adversarial perturbation. This involves computing the optimal perturbation and then updating the model's parameters based on the resulting gradient.

segments.subgoal: Explain how data biases create shortcuts and limit model generalization

key_points.text: Models often learn 'shortcuts,' which are features correlated with the label in training data but not under realistic distribution shifts.
Real-world data collection often results in noisy, complicated, and biased annotations, which limits the ability to construct a perfectly representative benchmark.
Data imbalance can cause models to learn correlative shortcuts, such as associating a species with a specific time of day.
Adversarial training helps models achieve invariance to non-robust features, making them more stable under perturbations.

key_terms.definition: Shortcut is a feature that is correlated with the label in the training data but is not correlated with the label under realistic distribution shifts. Models will use these shortcuts and fail to generalize if those features are no longer correlated.
Out-of-Distribution refers to data that falls outside the distribution of the data the model was trained on. This concept is contrasted with independently identically distributed data.
Adversarial examples are types of perturbations that can cause a model to misclassify an input. These examples can often transfer across models if they were trained on the same data set.

Adversarial training is a method used during model training to make the model robust to non-robust features and adversarial perturbations. This training aims to achieve invariance to these non-robust features.

segments.subgoal: Analyze how realistic distribution shifts, including subpopulation shift, impact model generalization

key_points.text: Distribution shift occurs when the distribution of data used for training is significantly different from the distribution used for inference (385).
Realistic distribution shifts are complex and can include visual changes (like camera pose or background) and subpopulation shifts (410-412, 417).
When models are tested on realistic, out-of-distribution data, their performance degrades significantly (402).
Model performance often correlates strongly with the similarity of subpopulation distributions between training and testing data (429).

key_terms.definition: Distribution shift occurs when the distribution of data used for training is different from the distribution of data encountered during inference. This difference means the model is operating in a different data environment than it was trained on.

Subpopulation shift occurs when any given location or camera has its own unique distribution over the categories of interest. This means the local set of species or features interacting with a specific point differs from the overall training set.

Out-of-distribution (OOD) refers to scenarios where the entire distribution of data used for inference is significantly different from the distribution encountered during training. OOD shifts are characterized by complex, realistic changes—such as background or camera pose variations—rather than simple, artificial perturbations applied to individual data points.

segments.subgoal: Explain Distributionally Robust Optimization (DRO) and its guarantees for generalization

key_points.text: Distributionally Robust Optimization (DRO) considers perturbing the entire training distribution, unlike adversarial examples which perturb individual data points.
DRO assumes the worst-case data distribution shift might occur, aiming to minimize loss in expectation over all possible shifts.
Measuring the distance between complex probability distributions (like large image datasets) is complicated, often requiring metrics like Wasserstein distance or learned representations.
If the new distribution where the model is used is within a certain distance of the true distribution, DRO guarantees good generalization performance.

key_terms.definition: Distributionally robust optimization is a method that assumes the worst-case data distribution shift might occur. It seeks to find a model that minimizes the loss in expectation over all possible distribution shifts on the dataset.

Distribution shift refers to the change in the data distribution between the training phase and the deployment phase. This shift can involve changes in the densities or the removal of samples from the original training data set.

Generalization is the ability of a model to perform well on the true distribution. This is guaranteed if the new distribution where the model is used is within a certain distance of the true distribution.

segments.subgoal: Explain how Distributionally Robust Optimization (DRO) addresses class imbalance and fairness

key_points.text: Standard models may ignore minority subgroups, resulting in low overall error even if the minority group's accuracy is poor.-
DRO automatically reweights data to force the model to pay more attention to minority classes.
DRO works by placing less emphasis on noisy features and shifting the distribution to make classes more separable.-
DRO is applied to fairness problems to prevent models from being biased against specific demographic groups.-

key_terms.definition: Class imbalance challenges occur when a dataset has a disproportionate number of examples in one category. This can cause a model to ignore minority groups and still achieve a decent overall loss.

segments.subgoal: Describe various strategies for improving model generalization against distribution shifts

key_points.text: One approach to distribution shift is using distributionally robust optimization or building extensions to make models more robust or fair.
Models can explicitly learn priors over distribution shifts, such as using spatiotemporal priors to remap likelihoods in species identification.
Domain adaptation is a category of models that aligns representations between a source and target domain to enforce generalization, even with limited target data.

key_terms.definition: Domain adaptation is a category of models that learns to align representations between a source domain and a target domain. This allows the model to generalize or adapt to a new target domain even if there is limited labeled data.

segments.subgoal: Evaluate the practical strategies for improving model robustness and generalization

key_points.text: Model failure modes can be diagnosed by breaking down evaluation across different dimensions, such as participant sex or time of day.
The most effective way to make a model robust is to use training data that is representative of the test domain.
If large-scale training data cannot be collected due to constraints (e.g., endangered species or deep sea environments), human review of the data is often required.
When time and effort are limited, labeling more data is often the most practical solution for improving model performance.

key_terms.definition: Failure mode refers to the specific ways a model performs poorly, which can be diagnosed to reveal underlying biases present in the initial training data.
In-distribution training data is the type of data that is representative of the domain where the model is expected to operate successfully.

The choice of activation functions (e.g., ReLU or GELU) is a topic of research regarding its effect on model generalization or robustness.
Generalizable robustness aims to be robust to any hypothetical change, whereas adaptation optimizes performance for a specific, known distribution shift.

key_terms.definition: Out-of-distribution generalization is the challenge of ensuring a model performs well when encountering data that differs from the data it was trained on. Digging into this challenge helps researchers understand what neural networks learn and how training data relates to effective model usage.

Distribution shifts represent changes in the data distribution, which can be addressed either by aiming for generalizably robust performance against any hypothetical change, or by specializing and adapting to a specific, known distribution shift.

objectives.text: You'll be able to analyze how distribution shifts and adversarial examples expose the brittleness and weaknesses of deployed machine learning models.

key_terms.definition: Adversarial examples are types of perturbations that can cause a model to misclassify an input. These examples can often transfer across models if they were trained on the same data set.

Perturbation is a small change applied to a given input image, which is designed to change the model's prediction without being noticeable to a human observer. This change is the variable that is optimized to maximize the model's misclassification.

Adversarial training is a method used during model training to make the model robust to non-robust features and adversarial perturbations. This training aims to achieve invariance to these non-robust features.

Projected gradient ascent is a technique used to update the data perturbation over time by taking a step in the direction of the gradient and then projecting the result back into a feasible set. This process ensures the perturbation obeys the optimization constraint that the change cannot be too big

Independently and Identically Distributed (IID) is a theoretical assumption in machine learning where the data used for training a model is drawn from the same distribution as the data used for inference. This ideal setting requires that the training distribution equals the test distribution, a condition the instructor notes is rarely true in the real world.

Decision support tools are machine learning systems that provide advice or highlight information, such as potential diagnoses. The human user is ultimately liable to verify the tool's output and make the final decision.

Subpopulation shift occurs when any given location or camera has its own unique distribution over the categories of interest. This means the local set of species or features interacting with a specific point differs from the overall training set.

Distributionally robust optimization is a method that assumes the worst-case data distribution shift might occur. It seeks to find a model that minimizes the loss in expectation over all possible distribution shifts on the dataset.

open_questions.reference_answer: The IID assumption posits that the training distribution equals the test distribution, meaning the data is independently and identically distributed. This shift can happen due to various factors, such as data becoming perturbed, changes in sensor manufacturers, or shifts in the set of categories of interest. Ultimately, we cannot possibly characterize and anticipate every way that the world is going to change.
